page: Vultr vhp-1c-1gb-amd is an entry-tier virtual server within the High Performance product line, powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor clocked at 2.0 GHz. The instance configuration allocates a single shared vCPU, 1.0 GB of system memory, and 25 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. The processor exposes vector compute extensions including AVX-512, AVX-512 VNNI, and AVX-512 BF16, alongside cryptographic instructions such as AES, VAES, and SHA-NI. The server includes one complimentary public IPv4 address and does not feature a dedicated GPU accelerator.

Benchmark results highlight strong single-core execution capacity on this AMD architecture, with the stress-ng single-core test reaching 3,294.99 points, placing it in the top tier of single-thread benchmarks. Multi-threaded operations remain limited by the single-core shared execution model, reflected in an overall PassMark CPU score of 2,738.52. Uncached memory read bandwidth achieves 36.16 GB/sec while write bandwidth maintains 29.11 GB/sec. File processing metrics remain stable in middle tiers, reaching 29.37 GB/sec in gzip compression and 13.19 GB/sec in bzip3 decompression, while concurrent networking tasks show 1.52 GB/sec in static web serving.

The combination of a single shared core and a 1.0 GB memory footprint provides a cost-effective resource tier for low-utilization tasks, though resource contention can occur under high tenant activity. The instance is not configured for high-concurrency databases or large memory caches. Vultr vhp-1c-1gb-amd is suited for development sandboxes, monitoring agents, automated background workers, low-volume cron tasks, and edge microservices.
description: Vultr vhp-1c-1gb-amd is an entry-level virtual server within the High Performance product line, powered by an x86_64 AMD EPYC processor operating at 2.0 GHz. The configuration provides 1 shared vCPU, 1.0 GB of RAM, and 25 GB of local NVMe SSD storage, without GPU acceleration. The underlying AMD architecture supports AVX-512 and hardware cryptographic instructions, enabling strong single-thread performance, evidenced by a stress-ng single-core score of 3,294.99. However, total compute and system throughput remain restricted by the single shared execution thread and limited memory allocation, yielding average write bandwidth of 29.11 GB/sec and lower throughput in memory-intensive operations. The instance delivers a cost-effective operational profile suitable for lightweight utility services, development environments, automation workers, low-traffic web endpoints, and microservices with modest memory demands.
